title: Pre-Race Dietary Carbohydrate Intake Can Independently Influence Sub-Elite Marathon Running Performance
authors: Atkinson G, Taylor CE, Morgan N, Ormond LR, Wallis GA
population: 257 competitors in the 2009 London Marathon (mean age 39 +/- 8 years, mean finish time 273.8 +/- 59.5 min) who logged anthropometry, training and nutrition online
findings: Sex, body mass index, training distance and the carbohydrate eaten the day before the race were significant predictors of running speed; together they accounted for 56% of the inter-individual variability (P < 0.0005).
The slope for the day-before carbohydrate was B = 0.08 to 0.26 km/h per unit.

Runners who ate more than 7 g/kg body mass of carbohydrate the day before had faster overall race speeds (P = 0.01) and kept their speed during the race to a greater extent (P = 0.02) than those who ate less than 7 g/kg.
The authors conclude that pre-race-day carbohydrate intake can independently influence marathon performance.
limitations: Observational with self-recorded diet and online data collection; the high-intake group may differ in other ways (a faster, more experienced group); the unit of the slope is not stated in the abstract; the finishing time of the mean runner (4.6 h) is slower than the typical engine goal.
implications: A day-before intake above about 7 g/kg went with faster marathon speed and less fade in 257 mostly slower runners. This sits under the existing K6 race-week carbohydrate line (8 to 10 g/kg); it supports the direction, not a higher number, and does not support in-race rates.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (IJSM 32:611-617). Abstract read on Europe PMC and PubMed (PubMed text used for the P values, which Europe PMC garbled). Crossref lists no correction, erratum or retraction notice (checked 2026-11-16).
